title: Environmental sustainability and CSR in operations

2026-10-29T14:30:28Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (b wording)

match.reason: The bank's CSR and triple bottom line points cover the general idea at Year 11 level, but none teaches sustainability and CSR applied to operations, including how they can also cut costs, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: Sustainability and CSR in operations
card: meeting present needs without harming the environment for the future. In operations, this means cutting waste, emissions and energy use.
a business acting ethically toward the community and its stakeholders. In operations, this includes treating workers and suppliers fairly, such as paying a fair price and keeping safe conditions.
Customers, investors and the community increasingly expect businesses to act this way. A business that ignores these expectations risks damage to its reputation.
Sustainable practices can also cut costs. Using less energy lowers power bills, and reducing waste means fewer materials are bought and thrown away.
draft.remember: Sustainability and CSR meet community expectations, and they can also lower operating costs.

a.q: Which action is an example of environmental sustainability in operations?
opts: A bakery installs equipment that uses less energy
A bakery pays its suppliers on time every month
A bakery trains staff in safe lifting techniques
A bakery sponsors a local junior football team
a.why: Using less energy cuts a business's impact on the environment. Paying suppliers on time is fair treatment, which is CSR, but it does not reduce the environmental impact of operations.
a.clue: Which action reduces waste, emissions or energy use?

b.q: Priya runs a furniture factory in Newcastle. She starts reusing timber offcuts to make small items, instead of sending them to landfill. Which outcome is most likely from this change?
opts: Less waste and lower material costs
Less waste but higher material costs
Fairer pay for workers in the factory
More electricity used by the factory
b.why: Reusing offcuts means less timber goes to landfill, and the business buys less new timber. The tempting option of higher costs is wrong because sustainable practices can save money, and here the saving comes from buying fewer materials.
b.clue: Think about what happens to the timber the business must buy.

a.best: A bakery installs equipment that uses less energy

b.best: Less waste and lower material costs

problems.detail: The scenario says Priya reuses offcuts to make small items. It does not say she used to buy new timber for those items, so it is unclear why she would buy less timber. The why claims 'the business buys less new timber', which the stem does not support. Say she uses offcuts for items she used to make from new timber, or mention avoided landfill fees, so 'lower material costs' clearly follows.

check.summary: Both answers are sound and the card is accurate. In question b, the stem should make clear that reusing offcuts replaces timber that would otherwise be bought, so the 'lower material costs' outcome clearly follows.

b.q: Priya runs a furniture factory in Newcastle. She used to make chopping boards from new timber. Now she makes them from offcuts that once went to landfill. Which outcome is most likely?
opts: Less waste and lower material costs
Less waste but higher material costs
Fairer pay for workers in the factory
More electricity used by the factory
b.why: The offcuts no longer go to landfill, so waste falls. Priya no longer buys new timber for the chopping boards, so her material costs fall. Higher costs is the tempting wrong option, but the offcuts replace timber she used to pay for.
b.clue: Think about the new timber she used to buy for the boards.
